summary: Reproduces an ISO protocol that lets end systems and intermediate systems exchange configuration and routing information. This helps the Network Layer do its routing and relaying work, and is meant to be used alongside ISO 8473 (CLNP). It is part of the OSI set of standards.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the OSI standard's counterpart to the way routers announce themselves on an IP network. A machine sends a Hello message on a regular timer to say that it exists and where it is attached, and a router that knows a shorter way to reach a destination sends a Redirect to point the way. The RFC is one of the OSI International Standards, reproduced here so that the protocol can be used with the connectionless network service ISO 8473.

how do end systems find routers in osi
subtitle: The OSI protocol that lets end systems and routers on one subnet find each other.

tldr.problem: In the OSI network layer, a machine attached to a subnet needs to know which routers on that subnet are there and reachable, and which other machines on the subnet are there. Otherwise it cannot decide where to send a packet.
tldr.mechanism: End systems and intermediate systems announce themselves to each other with Hello PDUs on a timer, and routers send Redirect PDUs to tell an end system about a shorter path. Every announcement carries a holding time, so stale information expires on its own.
tldr.outcome: Machines on a subnet discover each other and the routers between them without manual configuration, which is the part of routing the protocol deliberately leaves to another protocol, the one that runs among the routers themselves.

today: RFC 995 was published in April 1986 as the reproduction of the ISO International Standard for the End System to Intermediate System Routing Exchange Protocol, for use with ISO 8473. It has not been obsoleted or updated. The RFC states the protocol's limits itself: it covers only the part of routing between systems on one subnetwork, and the exchange of routing information among intermediate systems is left to a separate protocol.

sections.title: The Problem This Protocol Solves
sections.content:
This protocol is one of a set of International Standards produced to facilitate the interconnection of open systems, and it is positioned with respect to other related standards by the layers defined in the Reference Model for Open System Interconnection and by the structure defined in the Internal Organization of the Network Layer. It is a protocol of the Network Layer, and it permits End Systems and Intermediate Systems to exchange configuration and routing information to facilitate the operation of the routing and relaying functions of that layer.

The RFC draws an important distinction. The aspects of Network Layer routing concerned with communication between end systems and intermediate systems on the same subnetwork are to a great extent separable from the aspects concerned with communication among the intermediate systems that connect multiple subnetworks. This protocol addresses only the former, and will be significantly enhanced by the cooperative operation of an additional protocol that exchanges routing information among the intermediate systems, but it is useful whether or not such an additional protocol is available.

Four practical problems are listed. How do end systems discover the existence and reachability of intermediate systems that can route packets to destinations on subnetworks other than the one they are directly connected to? How do end systems discover the existence and reachability of other end systems on the same subnetwork, when direct examination of the destination address does not provide information about the destination subnetwork? How do intermediate systems discover the existence and reachability of end systems on each of the subnetworks to which they are directly connected? And how do end systems decide which intermediate system to use to forward packets to a particular destination when more than one is accessible?

The protocol assumes that routing to a point of attachment on the same subnetwork is carried out satisfactorily by the subnetwork itself, but that the subnetwork is not capable of routing on a global basis using the address alone. Consequently, it is not possible to use Application Layer communication to carry out the functions of this protocol. It is connectionless, and is designed to minimise the amount of state an end system needs before it can begin to communicate with others, to minimise the memory needed to store routing information in end systems, and to minimise the computational complexity of end system routing algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: Two questions have to be answered before a machine can send a packet: which routers can it use, and which other machines are on this cable. The network underneath cannot answer them, because it only knows about the local subnet. This protocol fills that gap, and deliberately leaves the harder question, how the routers talk to each other, to a different protocol.

sections.title: Where It Sits Among the OSI Standards
sections.content:
The standard specifies a protocol used by Network Layer entities operating ISO 8473 in end systems and intermediate systems to maintain routing information, and it relies on the provision of a connectionless-mode underlying service. It specifies the procedures for the transmission of configuration and routing information between those entities, the encoding of the protocol data units used to carry that information, the procedures for the correct interpretation of protocol control information, and the functional requirements for implementations claiming conformance.

The procedures are defined in terms of the interactions between end system and intermediate system network entities through the exchange of protocol data units, and the interactions between a network entity and an underlying service provider through the exchange of subnetwork service primitives. The protocol does not specify any protocol elements or algorithms for facilitating routing and relaying among intermediate systems; such functions are intentionally beyond its scope.

The referenced standards are the basic reference model ISO 7498 and its connectionless-mode addendum, the network service definition ISO 8348 and its addenda on connectionless-mode transmission and on network layer addressing, the connectionless network service protocol ISO 8473, the internal organization of the network layer DIS 8648, the OSI management framework working draft SC21/N965, and the local area networks standard DIS 8802. The document also notes that it is designed to operate in close conjunction with ISO 8473, and that since routing styles are usually closely related to communication styles, the information this protocol provides may or may not be appropriate for supporting routing functions when a network layer protocol other than ISO 8473 is used.
sections.plainLanguage: This is one piece of the OSI stack. It sits in the network layer, works with the connectionless network service standard, and assumes the connectionless style of communication throughout. The part of routing that happens between the routers themselves is left to a different protocol.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Information
sections.content:
The protocol provides two types of information to the network entities that support it. Configuration information permits end systems to discover the existence and reachability of intermediate systems, and permits intermediate systems to discover the existence and reachability of end systems. It allows systems attached to the same subnetwork to dynamically discover each other's existence and availability, which eliminates the need for manual intervention to establish the identity of the network entities that can be used to route packets. Configuration information also permits end systems to obtain information about each other in the absence of an available intermediate system.

Route redirection information allows intermediate systems to inform end systems of potentially better paths to use when forwarding packets to a particular destination. A better path could be another intermediate system on the same subnetwork as the end system, or the destination end system itself if it is on the same subnetwork as the source. Letting the intermediate systems inform the end systems of routes minimises the complexity of routing decisions in end systems and improves performance, because the end system may then use the better intermediate system or local subnetwork access for subsequent transmissions.

The two kinds of information are separable. A network entity may choose to support the configuration information, the route redirection information, neither, or both, and if the configuration information is supported it need not be employed over all the subnetworks to which the entity is attached.

The source and destination address parameters are OSI Network Service Access Point addresses, with syntax and semantics described in a separate standard. The underlying service required is a connectionless one, expressed through a small set of primitives: a request carrying a destination address, a source address, a quality of service and user data, and the matching indication. The protocol is designed to take advantage of subnetworks that support broadcast, multicast or other forms of multi-destination addressing, and it assumes that the destination address may be one of two multi-destination addresses: all End System Network entities, or all Intermediate System Network entities. Where a real subnetwork does not inherently support such transmission, a convergence function may be used to provide it.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two messages. One says who is here: the Hello messages that let machines and routers find each other. The other says use this way instead: the Redirect that a router sends when it knows a shorter path. An implementation may support either, both or neither.

sections.title: The Protocol Functions
sections.content:
Many of the protocol functions are timer based, meaning that they are executed on the expiry of a timer rather than on receipt of a PDU or the invocation of a service primitive. The two major timers are the Configuration Timer and the Holding Timer. The Configuration Timer is local to each system and drives the Report Configuration function; it determines how often a system re-reports its availability to the other systems on the same subnetwork. The shorter the Configuration Timer, the more quickly other systems learn that the reporting system has become available or unavailable, and that increased responsiveness must be traded off against increased use of resources in the subnetwork and in the recipient systems. The Holding Timer applies to both configuration information and route redirection information; its value is set by the source of the information and transmitted in the PDU, and the recipient is expected to retain the information no longer than the Holding Timer. Old configuration or redirection information must be discarded when the Holding Timer expires, to ensure the correct operation of the protocol.

The Report Configuration function is used by end systems and intermediate systems to inform each other of their reachability and current subnetwork address. It is invoked every time the local Configuration Timer expires, and also on receipt of a Query Configuration PDU from another end system. An end system constructs one End System Hello PDU for each address it serves and issues one unit data request with that PDU on each subnetwork to which it is attached. An intermediate system constructs a single Intermediate System Hello PDU containing its Network Entity Title and does the same on each of its subnetworks. In both cases the Holding Timer field is set to approximately twice the Configuration Timer, large enough that the information survives even if every other report is lost, and small enough that other systems respond in a timely fashion. The end system sends its Hello to the group address meaning all intermediate system network entities, so that a single transmission on a broadcast subnetwork reaches all of the active routers.

The Record Configuration function records what a Hello says into the local routing information base, and the Configuration Response function answers a Query Configuration PDU. The Flush Old Configuration function discards entries whose Holding Timer has expired.

The Request Redirect function belongs to the intermediate system. When a packet arrives from an end system on the local subnetwork, the function examines the router's own routing and relaying output, which names either the intermediate system to forward to or the destination end system, and then asks whether the source end system could have sent the packet directly to that entity. If the next hop is the destination system and it is directly reachable on the source's subnetwork, or the next hop is an intermediate system connected to the same subnetwork as the end system, a better path exists and the source should be told. The router then forwards the original packet normally, and constructs a Redirect PDU holding the destination address, the subnetwork address of the better next hop, the Network Entity Title of the intermediate system being redirected to unless the redirect is to the destination end system, the Holding Timer, and the quality of service, priority and security options copied from the original packet. If there are not enough resources to both forward the original packet and send a Redirect, the original packet is given preference.

The Record Redirect function exists only in end systems and is invoked whenever a Redirect PDU is received; it adds or replaces the redirection information in the local routing information base, the essential item being the mapping from a destination address to a subnetwork address, along with the priority, security and quality of service options and the holding time. The Refresh Redirect function renews that information, and Flush Old Redirect discards entries whose timer has expired. A Redirect PDU may safely be discarded if there is not enough memory to store it, since the original intermediate system will keep forwarding packets on behalf of that entity anyway.

The PDU Header Error Detection function protects against failure of a system caused by processing erroneous information in the PDU header. It is realized by a checksum computed over the entire header and verified at each point where the PDU is processed; if the calculation fails, the PDU must be discarded. The function is optional and selected by the originating entity, and when it is not used the checksum field is set to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything runs on timers. Each machine repeats its Hello on a timer of its own, and every Hello carries a holding time telling the others how long to believe it. A router that spots a shorter route forwards the packet normally and then, if it can, sends a Redirect telling the sender to use the other way next time.

sections.title: Which Functions Are Required
sections.content:
Implementations do not have to support all of the functions described in the protocol clause. The functions are divided into four categories. Type A functions must be supported in all cases. Type B functions must be supported by systems which implement the Configuration Information. Type C functions must be supported by systems which implement the Redirect Information. Type D functions are optional. If a PDU is received which invokes an optional function that is not implemented, that PDU is discarded.

The classification is given as a table. Report Configuration, Record Configuration and Flush Old Configuration are Type B and apply to both end systems and intermediate systems. Configuration Response and PDU Header Error Detection are Type A, the response function applying to end systems and the error detection to both. Query Configuration is Type B and applies to end systems. Request Redirect is Type C and applies to intermediate systems, while Record Redirect, Flush Old Redirect and the optional Refresh Redirect apply to end systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every system has to implement every part. The functions that keep the protocol working at all are required of everyone; the rest depend on whether a system does configuration, does redirection, or treats a part as optional. A message that asks for something the receiver has not implemented is simply thrown away.

sections.title: How the PDUs Are Encoded
sections.content:
All protocol data units contain an integral number of octets, numbered from one in the order in which they are put into the unit data. The bits in an octet are numbered from one to eight, where bit one is the low-order bit, and when consecutive octets represent a binary number the lower octet number has the most significant value. A PDU contains, in order, the fixed part, the Network address part, the Subnetwork address part if present, and the Options part if present.

The fixed part holds the parameters that occur frequently, including the type code of the PDU, and its length and structure are defined by that code. It is nine octets long: a Network Layer Protocol Identifier whose value is 1000 0010, which identifies this protocol; a Length Indicator giving the length of the whole PDU in octets with a maximum of 254, the value 255 being reserved for possible future extensions; a Version/Protocol Identifier Extension whose value is binary 0000 0001; a reserved octet that must be zero; a Type field in which the three high-order bits are zero; a Holding Time field of two octets; and a two-octet Checksum.

Three type codes are defined and all other values are reserved: the End System Hello PDU is 00010 in the five type bits, the Intermediate System Hello PDU is 00100 and the Redirect PDU is 00110. The network address part carries the addresses, the subnetwork address part carries the point of attachment, and the options part carries optional parameters, each encoded with a type, a length and a value. The options defined are security, quality of service maintenance and priority. The RFC notes that the encoding of the PDUs is compatible with that used in ISO 8473, and that the method used for describing that encoding is provisional, with member bodies asked to comment on whether another method, such as ASN.1 with an appropriate concrete syntax, would be preferable.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message has the same nine-octet header: which protocol this is, how long the whole message is, whether it is a Hello from an end system, a Hello from a router, or a Redirect, how long to believe it, and a checksum. After that come the addresses and any optional parameters such as priority and security.

viz.caption: THE THREE EXCHANGES OF THE PROTOCOL

messages.label: ESH PDU
messages.note: End System Hello, sent to the group address for all intermediate systems. One per address served, on each subnetwork.

messages.label: ISH PDU
messages.note: Intermediate System Hello, carrying the router's Network Entity Title, sent to the group address for all end systems.

messages.label: RD PDU
messages.note: Redirect, sent when the router knows the end system could have reached the destination directly, or through a router on its own subnet.

fields.name: Length Indicator
fields.desc: The length of the entire PDU in octets, maximum 254. The value 255 is reserved.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Three zero bits, then 00010 for an ESH PDU, 00100 for an ISH PDU and 00110 for an RD PDU.

fields.name: Holding Time
fields.desc: How long the recipient should keep the information. The sender sets it to about twice its own Configuration Timer.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Optional header error detection, computed over the whole header. Set to zero when not in use.
